One-time secrets

Send a password, API key or private note through a link that works exactly once. It’s encrypted in your browser — we only ever hold ciphertext we can’t read.

Links you created

Only the status is stored — never the secret or its key. Anonymous links are remembered in this browser only.

How it works

  • Your browser encrypts the secret with AES-256-GCM using a fresh random key.
  • The key goes only into the link, after the #. Browsers never send that part to any server.
  • We store ciphertext we can’t read. The first view deletes it for good.
  • A password adds PBKDF2 with 600,000 rounds, and 5 wrong guesses destroy the secret.

Safe with previews

Chat apps that preview links can’t burn your secret — the recipient has to tap Reveal.

Stop pasting passwords into chat

Messages sit in chat histories, email archives and backups for years. A one-time link keeps the secret out of all of them: once your recipient opens it, the encrypted copy on our server is erased, and the link becomes useless.

Can you read my secrets?

No. Encryption happens in your browser, and the key lives only in the part of the link after #, which browsers never transmit. The server only ever stores scrambled data. The code is open source — check assets/secret.js.

What if someone intercepts the link?

Whoever opens it first sees the secret — and the intended recipient will then see “already viewed”, so you’ll know. For sensitive secrets, add a password and share it through a different channel.

What happens after it expires?

The ciphertext is deleted within minutes of expiry, and the record of the link itself is removed after 30 days.
